event: The U.S. House of Representatives voted to pass a resolution limiting war powers and halting military operations in Iran.

framings.name: Constitutional Separation of Powers
framings.question: Did the president violate the Constitution and the 1973 War Powers Act by waging war without congressional authorization?
framings.key_claim: Trump's military campaign against Iran is unconstitutional because it was launched and sustained without a declaration of war or congressional authorization, in direct violation of Article I and the War Powers Resolution.
framings.description: This framing centers on the foundational legal question of which branch of government holds the authority to commit the nation to war. It treats the House vote as a legitimate and necessary exercise of Congress's constitutional role.
framings.emphasizes: The 60-day clock under the War Powers Act, the absence of any AUMF, the Declare War Clause of Article I, and the precedent set by prior war powers resolutions.
framings.downplays: The strategic or military rationale for the Iran campaign, the practical enforceability of the resolution, and the long history of presidents of both parties stretching war powers.
sample_headlines: House passes war powers resolution directing Trump to end hostilities with Iran (NPR)
House Votes to Restrain Trump's Iran War Powers in Bipartisan Rebuke (TIME)

carriers.name: Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-NY)
carriers.excerpt: "The framers gave Congress this authority because they believed no single person should have the power to take this nation to war alone."
carriers.role_evidence: Meeks sponsored H.Con.Res.38 and led the floor effort across multiple attempts, making him the primary legislative originator of this framing.

carriers.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA)
carriers.excerpt: "There's a law on the books. I don't see what's complicated about it."
carriers.role_evidence: Fitzpatrick introduced his own war powers resolution in April and voted for the final measure, amplifying the constitutional-compliance framing from the Republican side.

carriers.name: Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA)
carriers.excerpt: "Trump's military attack on Iran is illegal and unconstitutional. It was not approved by Congress."
carriers.role_evidence: Markey's early public statement framed the war as flatly illegal, helping establish the constitutional violation narrative before the House vote.

carriers.name: National Constitution Center
carriers.excerpt: "The recent military actions in Iran by Israel and the United States has reignited a simmering constitutional debate."
carriers.role_evidence: Published a widely-cited explainer grounding the debate in constitutional history, amplifying the legal framing to a broad civic audience.

carriers.name: NPR
carriers.excerpt: "Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Penn., told reporters after the vote he chose to support the resolution because, 'we have to follow the law.'"
carriers.role_evidence: NPR's straight-news coverage foregrounded the legal compliance argument, reaching a large national audience.

carriers.name: White House / Trump Administration
carriers.excerpt: "The White House has dismissed the Meeks resolution on legal grounds, characterizing it as an 'unconstitutional legislative veto' over executive authority."
carriers.role_evidence: The administration directly contested the constitutional framing by arguing the resolution itself is unconstitutional, inverting the legal argument.

framings.name: Negotiation Sabotage / Undermining the Commander-in-Chief
framings.question: Does passing this resolution damage U.S. leverage and sabotage ongoing peace negotiations with Iran?
framings.key_claim: The House vote is a reckless and unpatriotic act that strips the president of negotiating leverage at the most critical moment of peace talks, emboldening Iran and prolonging the conflict.
framings.description: This framing, championed by Trump and Republican leadership, casts the resolution not as a constitutional check but as a politically motivated act of sabotage that harms national security and peace prospects.
framings.emphasizes: The timing of the vote during active negotiations, the fragility of the ceasefire, the need for executive latitude in diplomacy, and the partisan motivation of Democrats.
framings.downplays: The legal basis of the War Powers Act, the 90+ days of unauthorized hostilities, and the economic suffering caused by the war itself.
sample_headlines: Trump lashes out at lawmakers who voted to rein in his Iran war powers (Washington Times)
House passes war powers resolution to end hostilities in Iran, weakens Trump's negotiating leverage (Washington Times)

carriers.name: Donald Trump / Truth Social
carriers.excerpt: "Yesterday, in a meaningless vote... to limit my War Powers, right in the middle of my final negotiations to end the War with the Islamic Republic of Iran."
carriers.role_evidence: Trump's Truth Social post was the primary origination point for the 'sabotage of negotiations' framing, setting the tone for all subsequent Republican messaging.

carriers.name: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA)
carriers.excerpt: "I think a war powers resolution right now is very untimely, and a very, very negative, and dangerous thing for the country."
carriers.role_evidence: As House Speaker, Johnson institutionalized this framing in official Republican leadership messaging, repeatedly warning the vote would 'weaken' Trump's negotiating hand.

carriers.name: Rep. Brian Mast (R-FL), House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair
carriers.excerpt: "They just want a stupid political vote, which is what this is. Weakens the president's hands as he's negotiating with Iran."
carriers.role_evidence: As Foreign Affairs Committee chair, Mast amplified the negotiation-sabotage framing with institutional authority and colorful rhetoric.

carriers.name: Secretary of State Marco Rubio
carriers.excerpt: "Rubio warned Wednesday... that the Iranians would think that the administration's 'hands are going to be tied.'"
carriers.role_evidence: Rubio's testimony before the House Foreign Affairs Committee gave the negotiation-sabotage framing official State Department backing.

carriers.name: Washington Times
carriers.excerpt: "It could deal a blow to the president's leverage to negotiate a peace deal with Iran that says the regime cannot have a nuclear weapon."
carriers.role_evidence: The Washington Times amplified the negotiation-leverage framing to a conservative readership, treating it as a credible strategic concern rather than mere spin.

framings.name: Economic Pain / Cost to Ordinary Americans
framings.question: Is the war's economic toll on American families — gas prices, inflation, supply disruptions — justification for ending it?
framings.key_claim: The Iran war has inflicted severe economic harm on American households through skyrocketing fuel prices and global supply disruptions, making the war politically and practically unsustainable.
framings.description: This framing, which crosses partisan lines, focuses on the material consequences of the conflict for everyday Americans rather than on legal or strategic abstractions. It was the key driver of Republican defections.
framings.emphasizes: Gas prices at $5+/gallon, fertilizer costs, the Strait of Hormuz closure, inflation, and constituent anger in swing districts.
framings.downplays: The security rationale for the war, Iran's nuclear program, and the constitutional legal debate.
sample_headlines: People are tired of $5 gallon gas and $6 gallon diesel (Rep. Massie, widely quoted)
Iran Conflict and the Strait of Hormuz: Impacts on Oil, Gas, and Other Commodities (CRS Report)

carriers.name: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY)
carriers.excerpt: "They're tired of $5 gallon gas and $6 gallon diesel, and fertilizer we can't afford to put on our fields in Kentucky."
carriers.role_evidence: Massie's post-vote statement became the most-quoted articulation of the economic pain framing, giving it a vivid, constituent-level voice from a Republican.

carriers.name: Rep. Tom Barrett (R-MI)
carriers.excerpt: "I think that people are frustrated, certainly," Barrett said when asked about the pain his constituents felt stemming from the war.
carriers.role_evidence: Barrett's constituent-focused explanation for his vote amplified the economic pain framing from a Midwestern Republican perspective.

carriers.name: Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-NY)
carriers.excerpt: "The people are tired of suffering because of his war of choice – suffering at the gas pump, suffering at the supermarkets."
carriers.role_evidence: Meeks wove the economic pain framing into his floor leadership, broadening the resolution's appeal beyond constitutional purists.

carriers.name: Wikipedia / 2026 Iran War Fuel Crisis
carriers.excerpt: "Gas prices have risen $1.16 a gallon in the United States since the start of the war."
carriers.role_evidence: The Wikipedia article aggregating fuel crisis data became a widely-cited reference point for the economic cost framing across media.

carriers.name: Congressional Research Service (CRS)
carriers.excerpt: "U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran since February 2026... have raised concern about oil and natural gas markets in relation to the Strait of Hormuz."
carriers.role_evidence: The CRS report gave the economic disruption framing official congressional research backing, used by lawmakers on both sides.

carriers.name: PBS NewsHour
carriers.excerpt: "Since the U.S. joined Israel in launching the Feb. 28 strikes on Iran, Americans have seen gas prices spike at the pumps, adding to inflationary pressure."
carriers.role_evidence: PBS's coverage consistently foregrounded the economic cost angle, reaching a broad public audience.

framings.name: Symbolic Gesture / Legislative Futility
framings.question: Does this vote actually change anything, or is it a performative act with no real-world consequence?
framings.key_claim: The House resolution is largely symbolic — it faces a Senate supermajority threshold it cannot clear, and even if it did, Trump would veto it, making the vote a political statement rather than a policy instrument.
framings.description: This framing, used across the ideological spectrum, focuses on the procedural and practical limits of the resolution. It is neither celebratory nor condemnatory — it is deflationary, questioning the vote's real-world impact.
framings.emphasizes: The Senate's 60-vote threshold, Trump's veto power, the concurrent vs. joint resolution distinction, and the lack of enforcement mechanism.
framings.downplays: The symbolic and political momentum value of the vote, its role in building pressure over time, and the inspector general review it coincided with.
sample_headlines: House passes war powers resolution to end hostilities with Iran — the vote marked a rare bipartisan rebuke of the war, but is mostly symbolic (NPR)
US House votes to end Trump's Iran war: Does it matter? (Al Jazeera)

carriers.name: NPR
carriers.excerpt: "The vote is mostly symbolic. Democrats, despite multiple attempts, have been unable to pass a war powers resolution through the Republican-led Senate."
carriers.role_evidence: NPR's lede explicitly labeled the vote 'mostly symbolic,' establishing this framing prominently in mainstream coverage.

carriers.name: Al Jazeera English
carriers.excerpt: "For now, the vote will remain largely symbolic because of Trump's own presidential veto power... even though it marks a significant reprimand by lawmakers."
carriers.role_evidence: Al Jazeera's explainer-format article ('Does it matter?') directly interrogated the vote's practical impact, amplifying the futility framing to an international audience.

carriers.name: Donald Trump / Truth Social
carriers.excerpt: "Yesterday, in a meaningless vote..."
carriers.role_evidence: Trump's own characterization of the vote as 'meaningless' amplified the symbolic-futility framing from the right, albeit for different rhetorical purposes.

carriers.name: TIME Magazine
carriers.excerpt: "...a largely symbolic rebuke directing the President to end hostilities with Iran."
carriers.role_evidence: TIME's framing in its headline and lede reinforced the symbolic-gesture narrative for a large general readership.

carriers.name: ms.now / NBC affiliate aggregator
carriers.excerpt: "Procedurally, there is some disagreement among scholars and lawmakers as to whether the resolution would even carry the force of law."
carriers.role_evidence: Noted the scholarly dispute over whether a concurrent resolution is even legally binding, deepening the futility framing.

framings.name: Bipartisan Crack-Up / GOP Rebellion
framings.question: Does this vote signal a meaningful fracture in Republican unity and a broader political realignment around the Iran war?
framings.key_claim: The House vote reveals a growing and politically significant Republican revolt against Trump's war, driven by constituent pressure and midterm anxiety, that could reshape the party's foreign policy posture.
framings.description: This framing treats the vote primarily as a political story about intra-party dynamics — the erosion of Trump's grip on House Republicans — rather than as a legal or strategic event. It is the dominant frame in political journalism.
framings.emphasizes: The four Republican defectors, the Speaker's failed attempt to cancel the vote, the Senate's 50-47 procedural advance, rising GOP constituent pressure, and midterm election calculus.
framings.downplays: The constitutional and legal substance of the War Powers Act, the human and economic costs of the war, and the resolution's practical enforceability.
sample_headlines: House votes to limit Trump's Iran war powers in remarkable rebuke (CNN)
House passes resolution to end Iran War, challenging Donald Trump (The Hill)

carriers.name: CNN Politics
carriers.excerpt: "The House passed a resolution on Wednesday to limit President Donald Trump's war powers in Iran, a significant rebuke to Trump and his handling of the conflict."
carriers.role_evidence: CNN's 'remarkable rebuke' framing in its headline and lede drove the bipartisan-crack-up narrative to a massive national audience.

carriers.name: The Hill
carriers.excerpt: "The vote also highlights an increasing willingness among GOP lawmakers to buck Trump on prominent issues as the midterm election season evolves."
carriers.role_evidence: The Hill explicitly connected the vote to midterm dynamics and a broader pattern of GOP defections, amplifying the intra-party fracture framing.

carriers.name: NBC News
carriers.excerpt: "The House offered a rare rebuke to President Donald Trump on Wednesday, passing a Democratic-led measure to end his war with Iran."
carriers.role_evidence: NBC's 'rare rebuke' framing centered the story on Trump's political standing rather than the legal or strategic substance.

carriers.name: Rep. Adam Smith (D-WA)
carriers.excerpt: "People are beginning to finally listen to the American people who don't support the war in Iran, and I think there's a growing number of Republicans who see how devastating the war has been."
carriers.role_evidence: Smith's public commentary before the final vote helped establish the narrative of a growing Republican crack-up weeks before it materialized.

carriers.name: House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY)
carriers.excerpt: "Republicans were 'cowardly' to pull the vote," said Jeffries and other caucus leaders in a joint statement.
carriers.role_evidence: Jeffries' messaging after the aborted May vote framed Republican leadership's procedural maneuver as evidence of a crack-up they were trying to hide.

framings.name: Executive Overreach / Imperial Presidency
framings.question: Does this episode represent a dangerous long-term expansion of unchecked presidential war-making power that threatens democratic governance?
framings.key_claim: Trump's unilateral war against Iran — and his administration's novel legal arguments to circumvent the War Powers Act — represent a historic escalation of executive war-making power that sets a dangerous precedent regardless of outcome.
framings.description: This framing, prominent in legal academia and civil liberties circles, zooms out from the immediate vote to the structural question of whether the presidency has permanently accumulated war powers that Congress can no longer effectively check.
framings.emphasizes: The administration's 'ceasefire reset' argument for the 60-day clock, the White House's claim that the concurrent resolution is an unconstitutional legislative veto, the history of presidential war powers expansion since WWII, and the inspector general review.
framings.downplays: The partisan politics of the vote, the economic costs, and the immediate tactical question of Iran negotiations.
sample_headlines: Does the War Powers Resolution debate take on a new context in the Iran conflict? (National Constitution Center)
Congress hasn't officially declared war since WWII. Here's how presidential war powers have played out since then (PBS/AP)

carriers.name: National Constitution Center
carriers.excerpt: "The recent military actions in Iran by Israel and the United States has reignited a simmering constitutional debate: the ability of the president to use military force without prior congressional approval."
carriers.role_evidence: The NCC was among the first institutions to frame the Iran conflict as a new chapter in the long-running imperial presidency debate, providing historical and legal context.

carriers.name: Rep. Jared Huffman (D-CA)
carriers.excerpt: "We're inching closer to having both chambers of Congress declare this an illegal war. That's huge."
carriers.role_evidence: Huffman's framing of the vote as a step toward declaring the war 'illegal' elevated the structural/precedent dimension of the debate.

carriers.name: Pentagon / State Dept. / USAID Inspectors General (joint review)
carriers.excerpt: "The Pentagon, State Department and USAID inspectors general have launched a joint review of the US war with Iran... mandated by law to probe overseas military operations that exceed 60 days."
carriers.role_evidence: The IGs' joint review announcement on the same day as the vote gave the executive-overreach framing official institutional weight, implying the administration had exceeded legal limits.

carriers.name: Matthew Green, Catholic University (political scientist)
carriers.excerpt: "Party loyalty is a powerful force on Capitol Hill, and Republican leaders... will be strongly incentivized to let the Trump White House use military force without congressional approval."
carriers.role_evidence: Green's expert commentary, cited by PolitiFact/PBS, framed the structural incentive problem that enables executive overreach regardless of party.

carriers.name: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
carriers.excerpt: "Hegseth also said he believed the 60-day clock 'reset' when Trump announced the cease-fire."
carriers.role_evidence: Hegseth's 'clock reset' argument was the administration's primary counter to the overreach framing, and its novelty was itself cited as evidence of overreach by critics.

framings.name: National Security Necessity / Iran as Existential Threat
framings.question: Was the military campaign against Iran a justified and necessary response to a decades-long adversary that declared war on America?
framings.key_claim: Iran has been a hostile actor against the United States for 47 years, and the military campaign was a necessary act of national defense that Congress is now recklessly trying to terminate before the job is done.
framings.description: This framing, advanced by Trump and Republican hawks, contextualizes the war not as an act of aggression but as a long-overdue response to Iranian hostility, framing the House vote as a dangerous capitulation to an enemy.
framings.emphasizes: Iran's 47-year history of hostility, the 'death to America' chants, Iran's nuclear program, the killing of Khamenei, and the administration's claim that Operation Epic Fury achieved its objectives.
framings.downplays: The economic costs of the war, the absence of congressional authorization, the fragility of the ceasefire, and the lack of a clear exit strategy.
sample_headlines: "Iran declared war on us 47 years ago. They chant 'death to America.' The president is trying to keep the people safe." — Speaker Mike Johnson
"I'm an American. I don't believe in getting hit and walking away." — Rep. Brian Mast

carriers.name: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA)
carriers.excerpt: "Remember… Iran declared war on us 47 years ago. They chant 'death to America.' The president is trying to keep the people safe."
carriers.role_evidence: Johnson's pre-vote press conference statement was the clearest articulation of the national security necessity framing from Republican leadership.

carriers.name: Rep. Brian Mast (R-FL)
carriers.excerpt: "I'm an American. I don't believe in getting hit and walking away and pretending as though it didn't happen."
carriers.role_evidence: As Foreign Affairs Committee chair, Mast consistently amplified the 'Iran as aggressor' framing, framing the war as a defensive response.

carriers.name: Trump Administration (Operation Epic Fury framing)
carriers.excerpt: "Johnson claimed all of the US objectives in Iran were 'well defined' and 'achieved.'"
carriers.role_evidence: The administration's official naming of the campaign ('Operation Epic Fury') and claims of mission accomplishment institutionalized the national security success narrative.

carriers.name: Washington Times
carriers.excerpt: "Trump is working to approve a memorandum of understanding with Iran... setting the table for final talks over Tehran's nuclear program."
carriers.role_evidence: The Washington Times amplified the national security framing by centering the nuclear program as the war's legitimate strategic objective.

carriers.name: Rep. Jared Golden (D-ME)
carriers.excerpt: Golden was the lone Democrat who initially voted against the war powers resolution, later reversing his position.
carriers.role_evidence: Golden's initial opposition from the Democratic side gave the national security necessity framing rare bipartisan credibility before he reversed course.

framings.name: Global Humanitarian and Economic Catastrophe
framings.question: What is the full human and global economic cost of the war, and does the House vote reflect a reckoning with those consequences?
framings.key_claim: The Iran war has triggered the largest oil supply disruption in history, thousands of civilian deaths, a global food and fuel crisis, and risks of worldwide recession — costs that the House vote implicitly acknowledges but that U.S. political coverage systematically underweights.
framings.description: This framing, more prominent in international and non-U.S. media, foregrounds the war's catastrophic global consequences — the Strait of Hormuz closure, Gulf humanitarian crises, European energy shock — as the essential context for the House vote.
framings.emphasizes: The IEA's 'largest supply disruption in history' characterization, civilian deaths, Gulf food and water crises, European stagflation risk, and the global scope of the conflict's fallout.
framings.downplays: U.S. domestic political dynamics, the constitutional debate, and the resolution's procedural limitations.
sample_headlines: US House votes to end Trump's Iran war: Does it matter? (Al Jazeera)
Israel/US-Iran conflict 2026: Reopening the Strait of Hormuz (UK House of Commons Library)

carriers.name: Al Jazeera English
carriers.excerpt: "The vote marks the first successful effort by lawmakers to force the US to end a conflict that has had mounting catastrophic effects, from thousands of civilian deaths to global trade disruptions."
carriers.role_evidence: Al Jazeera was among the first major outlets to frame the House vote explicitly against the backdrop of civilian deaths and global catastrophe, not just U.S. politics.

carriers.name: Wikipedia / Economic Impact of the 2026 Iran War
carriers.excerpt: "The 2026 Iran war... has led to what the International Energy Agency has characterized as the 'largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market.'"
carriers.role_evidence: The Wikipedia article aggregating IEA data and global economic impacts became a widely-shared reference amplifying the catastrophe framing.

carriers.name: UK House of Commons Library
carriers.excerpt: "Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz... has pushed up global oil and gas prices, benefiting both Russia and, temporarily, Iran."
carriers.role_evidence: The UK Parliament's official research briefing institutionalized the global economic catastrophe framing from an allied-nation perspective.

carriers.name: International Energy Agency (IEA)
carriers.excerpt: "The head of the International Energy Agency described the situation caused by the war as the 'greatest global energy security challenge in history.'"
carriers.role_evidence: The IEA's authoritative characterization of the crisis gave the humanitarian/economic catastrophe framing global institutional credibility.

carriers.name: The Globe and Mail
carriers.excerpt: "Gulf hostilities flared anew on Wednesday, with the U.S. military saying Iranian missile attacks on Bahrain, Kuwait and other regional targets were either thwarted or failed."
carriers.role_evidence: The Globe and Mail's coverage consistently embedded the House vote within the ongoing regional military violence, amplifying the humanitarian cost framing to a Canadian/international audience.
